title: How can an output commit to several ways of spending?
dek: A coin can have several spending conditions. Taproot lets a spend reveal just the route it takes, while the unused alternatives stay hidden.

blocks.text: Imagine money that its owners can spend together, with a backup route if someone disappears: wait for a timeout, or use another key. Those alternatives are useful to the owners. An observer of the blockchain does not need to learn every one of them each time the money moves.

Taproot puts a public key in the output. That key can also commit to a tree of alternative spending scripts. When the owners use the key, they supply a signature. When they use a script, they reveal that script and a proof that it belongs to the commitment. The unused scripts can stay private.

figure.title: What reaches the blockchain
figure.caption: The same output, spent two ways. A key-path spend reveals no script tree. A script-path spend reveals the chosen script and enough hashes to prove its place.

sections.heading: Start with what an observer learns

blocks.text: The output key is already public before any spend happens. Using the key path adds a signature, with an optional annex discussed below. It does not publish the internal key or the script tree. From that spend alone, an observer cannot tell whether any alternative script existed.

This also works with arrangements in which several people jointly control a key. BIP 341’s authors envisioned agreement between all participants as a common route, leaving more complicated conditions for exceptional cases. Key aggregation lets their cooperative signature look like another single-key signature.

Taking the script path changes the disclosure. Now the script is public, along with a proof connecting it to the output. The proof reveals the script’s depth in the tree. It can include hashes of other branches, but a hash does not tell the observer what the hidden script says.

That distinction is the point of the interactive tree. First look at everything the wallet knows. Then pick a spending path and switch to the proof view. Watch how much disappears. The two views describe different knowledge about the same output.

blocks.title: Choose a path, then hide the rest
blocks.caption: The wallet knows the whole tree. The blockchain receives only the material needed for the selected spending path.

sections.heading: How a branch can stand for a whole tree

blocks.text: Each alternative script is a leaf. Hash the leaf’s version and script, including its length, to give it a compact identifier. Hash pairs of identifiers together, then repeat until only a root remains. A change to a script changes the commitment calculated above it.

To prove that a leaf belongs to this tree, you do not need to supply all the other leaves. Supply a sibling hash at each level instead. Starting with the revealed script, the verifier can hash its way back to the root. A whole hidden subtree can be represented by its one root hash.

There is no mandatory tree shape. BIP 341 suggests a balanced tree when the alternatives are equally likely, or a Huffman tree that puts likely scripts nearer the top. Those are wallet-design suggestions. A shallower leaf needs fewer sibling hashes, so its proof takes less space.

blocks.title: A deeper leaf needs a longer proof
blocks.caption: Each extra level contributes another 32-byte sibling hash.

blocks.text: The example has leaf A closer to the root than leaves B and C. Choosing A therefore produces a shorter control block. This is a tradeoff the wallet can make before the output is created; it cannot later move a leaf to a different depth without changing the commitment.

sections.heading: Where the tree meets the key

blocks.text: So far we have a tree root and an ordinary public key. Taproot combines them. The ordinary key is called the internal key, P. A hash of P and the root produces a tweak, t. Adding t⋅G to P gives a new point, Q, whose x coordinate becomes the output’s 32-byte witness program.

blocks.title: The tree changes the output key
blocks.caption: The internal key becomes a different output key after tweaking. The lower example includes a script tree; the upper one has no scripts.

blocks.text: The tree is now tied to the key on the blockchain, even though it was never published. A script-path verifier must reconstruct both the root and the tweaked output key. Producing a plausible-looking tree is not enough: the result must match the particular output being spent.

The key path remains available because the corresponding private key can be tweaked too. After accounting for the internal point’s y parity, its holder adds the same tweak to the private key and can sign for Q. The public calculation and the signing calculation arrive at the same output key.

blocks.summary: Outputs without scripts, older nodes and key aggregation

blocks.text: A Taproot output is exactly that: a native SegWit output with version 1 and a 32-byte program. Version 1 outputs of other lengths, and version 1 programs wrapped in P2SH, are left unencumbered by these rules. Nodes that never upgraded treat every version 1 program as anyone-can-spend, so these rules are enforced by upgraded nodes.

When there are no scripts, BIP 341 recommends that wallets still tweak the internal key, hashing P alone. Its authors explain why: if the output key is an aggregate of several parties’ keys, a malicious party could add a script path the others do not notice, bypass the shared policy and steal the coin. MuSig aggregation avoids that particular problem because it already randomizes the internal key. The no-script example above follows the wallet recommendation.

Aggregation is not a matter of adding public keys together by hand: a plain sum is open to key cancellation and related attacks unless something like a proof of possession guards it. BIP 341 points to protocols such as MuSig and leaves their details out of scope, and recommends making the most likely single-key condition the internal key.

sections.heading: Check the proof, then run the script

blocks.text: A script-path witness carries the script’s inputs, the script, and a control block. The block supplies the internal key and the sibling hashes. It also records the leaf version and one bit of information about the output key’s y coordinate. These pieces let the verifier repeat the commitment calculation.

blocks.title: What the two witnesses carry
blocks.caption: After removing any annex, one item selects the key path. Two or more select the script path.

blocks.text: First hash the revealed leaf. Join it to its sibling hash, and keep going up the proof. At each join the hashes are sorted before hashing, so the proof does not need left-or-right directions. Use the reconstructed root and internal key to calculate the tweak and output key.

blocks.title: Walk the proof back to the output
blocks.caption: Follow leaf B upward. Each sibling hash gets the verifier one step closer to the committed root.

blocks.text: Both the x coordinate and the parity bit must match. A proof for another script cannot simply be borrowed: changing the script, the parity bit or the expected output breaks the comparison. The parity bit pins down the exact curve point, which the authors need for batch verification.

Even a correct proof does not make the spend valid on its own. It establishes that this script was committed to. The script must still execute successfully with the remaining witness items as its starting stack. Leaf version 0xc0 uses the Tapscript rules in BIP 342.

blocks.summary: Control-block lengths, annexes and byte order

blocks.text: A verifier decides which path is being used by counting witness elements. None at all fails. If the last of two or more elements begins with the byte 0x50, it is set aside as the annex, a field reserved for future extensions that users SHOULD NOT include until a soft fork defines it. One remaining element means a key path spend; two or more mean a script path spend.

The script path carries more. The second-to-last element is the script, and the last is a control block of 33 + 32m bytes, where m runs from 0 to 128. Its first byte holds the leaf version, with the lowest bit recording whether Q has an even or odd y coordinate. The next 32 bytes are the internal key, followed by m sibling hashes, one per level. In vector 5 that makes 65 bytes for leaf A and 97 for B and C.

The wallet vectors write every hash as a byte array, first byte first. That is the opposite of the familiar convention for transaction IDs, which are displayed reversed. This page follows the vectors.

This page’s model reproduces every value the vectors publish: leaf hashes, roots, tweaks, output keys, scriptPubKeys and control blocks for all 7 trees, and the keys, tweaks, signature message, signature hash and signature for all 7 key-path inputs.

sections.heading: The signature also commits to the payment

blocks.text: Hiding unused conditions is only part of BIP 341. The signature message changes too. Unless the signer selects ANYONECANPAY, it commits to the amount and scriptPubKey of every output being spent. This gives an offline signer a commitment to all the input amounts when it checks the fee.

blocks.title: The amounts travel into the signature
blocks.caption: The outlined fields commit to every spent output’s amount and scriptPubKey in this example.

blocks.text: The authors designed that change to prevent a signing device being misled about the fee or the outputs it is spending. It is a separate benefit from revealing fewer scripts: one concerns the transaction the owner authorizes, the other concerns what observers learn afterwards.

Taproot still leaves clues. A script-path spend reveals its chosen condition and depth, and a distinctive tree can hint at the software that built it. Reusing keys creates other links; the BIP says keys should never be reused, and that covers every leaf committed to in the output, not only the one spent. The useful promise is narrower disclosure of spending conditions, not blanket anonymity.

A Taproot signature is a BIP 340 signature over a tagged hash, TapSighash, of a signature message. It is 64 bytes, or 65 with an explicit sighash byte; leaving the byte off means SIGHASH_DEFAULT, which signs the whole transaction like SIGHASH_ALL. Spelling out 0x00 as a 65th byte is invalid.

The signature message is at most 206 bytes; the illustrated input’s message is 174 bytes. BIP 341 was assigned in 2020 and records mainnet activation at block 709632. The figures use its published wallet vectors.
